missing_features.feature: Push notifications + reminder delivery (web push/FCM with email fallback) for expiring IDs, calendar events, chat messages, and shopping-list changes
missing_features.seen_in: Every competitor: Cozi, FamilyWall, TimeTree, Maple, OurHome, Trustworthy ('automated Reminders' is a headline feature)
missing_features.why_it_matters: This is the #1 thing reviewers will miss. Family Hub's expiry warnings and family chat only work if you happen to open the app — a chat nobody is notified about is dead on arrival, and 'we remind you before your passport expires' is only true if the reminder reaches the user. Firestore + Cloud Run makes FCM web push plus a daily email digest very feasible.

missing_features.feature: Recurring events on the calendar (weekly/monthly/annual with end dates and exceptions)
missing_features.seen_in: Cozi, TimeTree, FamilyWall, Google Calendar — universal table stakes in any calendar UI
missing_features.why_it_matters: The first real event a family adds is 'soccer practice every Tuesday.' If they must re-enter it weekly, the calendar is abandoned in week two. Birthdays already imply annual recurrence, so the model is half-built.

missing_features.feature: External calendar sync: subscribe-to iCal feed out, Google Calendar import/2-way sync in
missing_features.seen_in: TimeTree, Cozi, Maple, FamilyWall all import/sync external calendars; 2026 comparison articles use cross-calendar sync as a scoring criterion
missing_features.why_it_matters: Families already live in Google/Apple calendars; nobody re-types their life into a new app. A read-only iCal export URL per family is cheap and makes Family Hub's calendar visible where people already look. Without it the calendar competes with, rather than complements, their existing one.

missing_features.feature: Polished invite + onboarding flow: invite by link/email with role pre-assigned, guided first-run (add members, scan first document), empty states that teach
missing_features.seen_in: All consumer family apps; Trustworthy's onboarding walks you through categories; FamilyWall/Cozi have one-tap join links
missing_features.why_it_matters: Multi-family with roles already exists in the data model, but launch success hinges on the second family member actually joining. If the admin can't send a link that lands the spouse in the right family with the right role in under a minute, retention dies at day one. Also the moment to showcase the AI scan flow.

missing_features.feature: Security trust package: 2FA option, biometric/passcode re-lock before opening the passwords vault and ID documents, session re-auth, and a plain-language security/encryption statement page
missing_features.seen_in: Trustworthy (advertises 'advanced security & privacy'), 1Password, Dossier (FaceID vault lock), NordPass; digital-vault buying guides list MFA + AES-256 + access logs as must-haves
missing_features.why_it_matters: Family Hub stores passports, medical data, and passwords — the exact categories where reviewers ask 'is it encrypted, and what happens if my phone is grabbed while unlocked?' Google sign-in alone leaves the vault open behind an unlocked screen. A re-auth gate on the vault plus a credible security page is the minimum bar to be trusted with this data class; client-side encryption of the passwords vault is the stretch goal.

missing_features.feature: Data export / takeout: full-family ZIP+JSON export and a printable 'emergency dossier' PDF (per-member medical + contacts + IDs)
missing_features.seen_in: Trustworthy ('Download your information' on every plan), Dossier's emergency PDF export, Travel Document Vault; AARP/vault guides list export as a must-have
missing_features.why_it_matters: Two wins in one: it defuses the lock-in objection that kills trust in new vault apps ('what if this app disappears?'), and the printable emergency PDF extends the existing Emergency view to the offline, hand-it-to-the-babysitter/paramedic scenario. Cheap to build off data that is already structured.

missing_features.feature: Offline access to the Emergency view + PWA installability (manifest, service worker, cached emergency card)
missing_features.seen_in: Trustworthy ('mobile offline mode' on all plans), Medical ID / ICE apps (lock-screen and offline access is their whole category)
missing_features.why_it_matters: Emergency info that requires a network connection and a login fails precisely when it's needed. Caching the emergency card in a service worker and making the app installable to the home screen closes the biggest credibility gap of the Emergency feature and gets an app-like icon without app-store cost.

missing_features.feature: Expiring secure share links for a single document or the emergency card (share with school, babysitter, accountant — outside the family account)
missing_features.seen_in: Trustworthy SecureLinks™ (a flagship, trademarked feature); Travel Document Vault share/export
missing_features.why_it_matters: The real-world job is often 'send the insurance card to the school office' — recipients won't create accounts. Time-limited signed URLs (Firebase Storage already supports them) replicate Trustworthy's marquee premium feature at low cost and create a viral surface: every shared link advertises the app.

missing_features.feature: General to-dos/chores with assignment to members (beyond the shopping list), optionally with kid-friendly points/rewards
missing_features.seen_in: OurHome (points + rewards core loop), Maple (task manager + chore tracker), Cozi (to-dos), FamilyWall
missing_features.why_it_matters: Task lists are the daily-active-use engine of every family organizer — documents and IDs are touched monthly, chores daily. Family Hub already has a 'child' role with nothing for children to do; a simple assignable-task module (points optional, later) gives the child role a purpose and a reason to open the app between document scans.

missing_features.feature: Sign-in methods beyond Google: email/password (or magic link) and Sign in with Apple
missing_features.seen_in: All competitors offer email signup; Apple requires 'Sign in with Apple' for any iOS app offering third-party login
missing_features.why_it_matters: Google-only sign-in blocks the grandparent without a Google account and the iOS-heavy household, and is a hard App Store rejection if a native wrapper is ever shipped. Firebase Auth makes adding both providers configuration-plus-UI work.

missing_features.feature: Multiple named shopping lists with categories/aisles and real-time check-off (groceries vs pharmacy vs hardware)
missing_features.seen_in: AnyList (category/aisle sorting is its core value), Cozi (multiple lists + premade lists), FamilyWall, Maple
missing_features.why_it_matters: A single flat shopping list looks like a demo next to AnyList. Category grouping and multiple lists are small schema changes with outsized perceived polish; real-time check-off while a partner shops is the moment sync visibly 'wows'. AI could auto-categorize items as the differentiating twist.

missing_features.feature: App-store presence via a thin native wrapper (Capacitor) — post-launch, after PWA install is solid
missing_features.seen_in: Every competitor is on the App Store/Play Store; discovery for 'family organizer' happens almost entirely in app-store search
missing_features.why_it_matters: A web-only PWA forfeits the primary discovery channel and the perception of legitimacy for an app asking for passports and medical data. Not a launch blocker (PWA first is fine for the initial cohort), but the roadmap item that most affects growth; also unlocks reliable push on iOS.

missing_features.feature: Meal planning / recipe box (deliberately deferred — cover via AI instead)
missing_features.why_it_matters: It's the most common competitor feature Family Hub lacks, so reviewers doing checkbox comparisons will note it — but it's a different job-to-be-done (daily coordination) than the vault core. Rather than building a full planner pre-launch, let the AI chatbot generate a week's meals into the shopping list as a demo of the AI angle, and defer the dedicated module.

positioning_notes: The 2026 market is cleanly split into two price bands, and Family Hub straddles them — which is the opportunity. Daily-coordination apps (calendar/lists/chores) charge $0–$80/yr: Cozi Gold $39/yr and Cozi Max $79.99/yr (AI), FamilyWall $4.99/mo, TimeTree ~$45/yr, Maple free tier + ~$40–68/yr for its AI assistant, OurHome free, AnyList ~$40/yr family. Vault/records apps charge much more: Trustworthy — the closest direct competitor and the category-definer ('Family Operating System') — runs Free (2GB) / Silver $120/yr / Gold $240/yr / Platinum $480/yr, and notably paywalls its AI auto-organization and 'ask your documents' chat at the $240/yr Gold tier; 1Password Families is $71.88/yr for credentials only. Everything with AI in this space is subscription, not one-off, and Family Hub's Gemini proxy has real per-use cost — so a one-off price is not viable; the model should be freemium (1 family, limited AI scans, capped storage) plus a single per-family (not per-seat) subscription around $50–70/yr, deliberately undercutting Trustworthy Gold by 3–4x while sitting just above Cozi. The single strongest positioning angle is the AI scan-anything-in flow: 'the family vault that fills itself' — photograph a passport, insurance letter, or utility bill and the AI files it into the right member's profile with expiry tracking, the exact capability Trustworthy charges $240/yr for, delivered at Cozi's price and in 9 languages (a genuine wedge for multilingual/immigrant and expat families, whom the US-centric incumbents ignore). Lead marketing with the scan-to-structured-data demo video; the prerequisite is closing the trust gap first (security page, vault re-lock, export), because the pitch only works if people believe the vault is safe.
